            <div role="main"><div id="mod_book-chaptersnavigation"><div class="container-fluid tertiary-navigation">
    <div class="row">
            <div class="navitem">
                <a class="btn btn-link btn-previous" href="https://learn.saylor.org/mod/book/view.php?id=96106&amp;chapterid=90519#mod_book-chapter" title="Previous" aria-label="Previous">
                    <i class="icon fa fa-chevron-left fa-fw " aria-hidden="true" ></i>
                </a>
            </div>
    </div>
</div></div><div id="mod_book-chapter" class="box py-3 generalbox book_content"><h3>Hashing I</h3><div class="no-overflow"><span class="filter_mathjaxloader_equation"><h4 dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Lecture Overview&nbsp;</h4><ul dir="ltr"><li style="text-align: left;">Dictionaries and Python</li><li style="text-align: left;">Motivation</li><li style="text-align: left;">Prehashing</li><li style="text-align: left;">Hashing</li><li style="text-align: left;">Chaining&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;">Simple uniform hashing</li><li style="text-align: left;">"Good" hash functions&nbsp;</li></ul><h3 dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;"><br></h3><h3 dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Dictionary Problem</h3><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Abstract Data Type (ADT) - maintain a set of items, each with a key, subject to&nbsp;</p><ul dir="ltr"><li style="text-align: left;">insert(item): add item to set</li><li style="text-align: left;">delete(item): remove item from set</li><li style="text-align: left;">search(key): return item with key if it exists&nbsp;</li></ul><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">We assume items have distinct keys (or that inserting new one clobbers old).
Balanced BSTs solve in <span class="nolink">\(O(lg \; n)\)</span> time per op. (in addition to inexact searches like next-
largest).&nbsp;</p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Goal: <span class="nolink">\(O(1)\)</span> time per operation.&nbsp;</p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;"><br></p><h3 dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Python Dictionaries:</h3><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Items are (key, value) pairs e.g. d = {'algorithms': 5, 'cool': 42}&nbsp;</p><div style="margin-left: 30px;" class="editor-indent">d.items() → [('algorithms', 5),('cool',5)]&nbsp;<br>d['cool'] → 42&nbsp;<br>d[42] → KeyError&nbsp;<br>'cool' in d → True&nbsp;<br>42 in d → False <br></div><div style="margin-left: 30px;" class="editor-indent"><br></div><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Python <u>set </u>is really <u>dict </u>where items are keys (no values)<br></p>
<p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;"><br></p><h3 dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Motivation</h3><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Dictionaries are perhaps the most popular data structure in CS&nbsp;</p><ul dir="ltr"><li style="text-align: left;">built into most modern programming languages (Python, Perl, Ruby, JavaScript,
Java, C++, C#, . . . )&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;">e.g. best docdist code: word counts &amp; inner product&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;">implement databases: (DB HASH in Berkeley DB)<ul><li style="text-align: left;">English word → definition (literal dict.)&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;">English words: for spelling correction&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;">word → all webpages containing that word&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;">username → account object&nbsp;</li></ul></li><li style="text-align: left;">compilers &amp; interpreters: names → variables&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;">network routers: IP address → wire&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;">network server: port number → socket/app.</li><li style="text-align: left;">virtual memory: virtual address → physical&nbsp;</li></ul><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Less obvious, using hashing techniques:&nbsp;</p><ul dir="ltr"><li style="text-align: left;">substring search (grep, Google) [L9]</li><li style="text-align: left;">string commonalities (DNA) [PS4]</li><li style="text-align: left;">file or directory synchronization (rsync)&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;">cryptography: file transfer &amp; identification [L10] </li></ul><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;"><br></p><h3 dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">How do we solve the dictionary problem?</h3><h4 dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Simple Approach: Direct Access Table</h4><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">This means items would need to be stored in an array, indexed by key (random access)</p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><img src="https://learn.saylor.org/pluginfile.php/10439570/mod_book/chapter/90520/Screenshot%202024-04-27%20at%2007-57-01%206.006%20Lecture%2008%20Hashing%20with%20chaining%20-%20d3e4d64266d481c74c9e7c15e09999fe_MIT6_006F11_lec08.pdf.png" alt="Figure 1: Direct-access table" width="230" height="247" class="img-fluid atto_image_button_text-bottom"><br></p>
<p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><strong>Figure 1:</strong> Direct-access table</p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Problems:&nbsp;</p><ol dir="ltr"><li style="text-align: left;">keys must be nonnegative integers (or using two arrays, integers)</li><li style="text-align: left;">large key range =⇒ large space - e.g. one key of 2<sup>256</sup> is bad news.&nbsp;</li></ol><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">2 Solutions:&nbsp;</p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;"><em>Solution to 1 : "prehash" keys to integers.&nbsp;</em></p><ul dir="ltr"><li style="text-align: left;">In theory, possible because keys are finite =⇒ set of keys is countable&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;">In Python: <u>hash</u>(object) (actually hash is misnomer should be "prehash") where
object is a number, string, tuple, etc. or object implementing _ _hash_ _ (default = id
= memory address)&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;">In theory, x = y ⇔ hash(x) = hash(y)&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;">Python applies some heuristics for practicality: for example, hash('\0B ') = 64 =
hash('\0\0C')&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;">Object's key should not change while in table (else cannot find it anymore)</li><li style="text-align: left;">No mutable objects like lists&nbsp;</li></ul><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;"><em>Solution to 2 : hashing (verb from French 'hache' = hatchet, &amp; Old High German 'happja'
= scythe)</em></p><ul dir="ltr"><li style="text-align: left;">Reduce universe <span class="nolink">\(U\)</span> of all keys (say, integers) down to reasonable size m for table</li><li style="text-align: left;"><u>idea</u>: m ≈ n = # keys stored in dictionary&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;"><u>hash function</u> h: <span class="nolink">\(U → {0, 1, . . . , m − 1}\)</span></li></ul>
<p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><img src="https://learn.saylor.org/pluginfile.php/10439570/mod_book/chapter/90520/Screenshot%202024-04-27%20at%2007-57-47%206.006%20Lecture%2008%20Hashing%20with%20chaining%20-%20d3e4d64266d481c74c9e7c15e09999fe_MIT6_006F11_lec08.pdf.png" alt="Figure 2: Mapping keys to a table " width="456" height="189" class="img-fluid atto_image_button_text-bottom"><br></p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><strong>Figure 2: </strong>Mapping keys to a table&nbsp;</p><ul dir="ltr"><li style="text-align: left;">two keys <span class="nolink">\(k_i\)</span>, <span class="nolink">\(k_j ∈ K\)</span> <u>collide </u>if <span class="nolink">\(h(k_i) = h(k_j)\)</span></li></ul><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;"><br></p><h5 dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;"><u>How </u>do we deal with collisions?</h5><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">We will see two ways&nbsp;</p><ol dir="ltr"><li style="text-align: left;">Chaining: TODAY&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;">Open addressing: L10&nbsp;</li></ol><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;"><br></p><h3 dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Chaining</h3><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Linked list of colliding elements in each slot of table<br></p>
<p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><img src="https://learn.saylor.org/pluginfile.php/10439570/mod_book/chapter/90520/Screenshot%202024-04-27%20at%2007-58-40%206.006%20Lecture%2008%20Hashing%20with%20chaining%20-%20d3e4d64266d481c74c9e7c15e09999fe_MIT6_006F11_lec08.pdf.png" alt="Figure 3: Chaining in a Hash Table" width="467" height="164" class="img-fluid atto_image_button_text-bottom"><br></p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><strong>Figure 3: </strong>Chaining in a Hash Table</p><ul dir="ltr"><li style="text-align: left;">Search must go through whole list T[h(key)]&nbsp;</li><li style="text-align: left;">Worst case: all n keys hash to same slot ⇒ Θ(n) per operation</li></ul>
<p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;"><br></p><h3 dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Simple Uniform Hashing:</h3><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">An assumption (cheating): Each key is equally likely to be hashed to any slot of table,
independent of where other keys are hashed.&nbsp;</p><p style="margin-left: 30px;" class="editor-indent">let n = # keys stored in table <br></p><p style="margin-left: 30px;" class="editor-indent">m = # slots in table <br></p><p style="margin-left: 30px;" class="editor-indent"><u>load factor</u> α = n/m = expected # keys per slot = expected length of a chain<br></p><br><h4 dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Performance</h4><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">This implies that expected running time for search is <span class="nolink">\(Θ(1+α)\)</span> - <em>the 1 comes from applying
the hash function and random access to the slot</em> whereas the <em>α comes from searching the
list</em>. This is equal to <span class="nolink">\(O(1)\)</span> if <span class="nolink">\(α = O(1)\)</span>, i.e., <span class="nolink">\(m = Ω(n)\)</span>. <br></p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;"><br></p><h3 dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Hash Functions</h3><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">We cover three methods to achieve the above performance:&nbsp;</p><h4 dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Division Method:</h4><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><em>h(k) = k mod m</em></p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">This is practical when m is prime but not too close to power of 2 or 10 (then just depending
on low bits/digits).&nbsp;</p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">But it is inconvenient to find a prime number, and division is slow.&nbsp;</p><h4 dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Multiplication Method:</h4><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><span class="nolink">\(h(k) = [(a · k) \text{ mod } 2^w] &gt; (w − r)\)</span></p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">where <span class="nolink">\(a\)</span> is random, <span class="nolink">\(k\)</span> is <span class="nolink">\(w\)</span> bits, and <span class="nolink">\(m = 2^r\)</span>.</p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">This is practical when <span class="nolink">\(a\)</span> is odd &amp; <span class="nolink">\(2^{w−1} &lt; a &lt; 2^w\)</span> &amp; <span class="nolink">\(a\)</span> not too close to <span class="nolink">\(2^{w−1}\)</span> or <span class="nolink">\(2^w\)</span>.<br></p>
<p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Multiplication and bit extraction are faster than division.<br></p>
<p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><img src="https://learn.saylor.org/pluginfile.php/10439570/mod_book/chapter/90520/Screenshot%202024-04-27%20at%2008-00-53%206.006%20Lecture%2008%20Hashing%20with%20chaining%20-%20d3e4d64266d481c74c9e7c15e09999fe_MIT6_006F11_lec08.pdf.png" alt="Figure 4: Multiplication Method" width="447" height="267" class="img-fluid atto_image_button_text-bottom"><br></p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><strong>Figure 4:</strong> Multiplication Method</p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><br></p><h4 dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">Universal Hashing</h4><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">[6.046; CLRS 11.3.3]</p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">For example: <span class="nolink">\(h(k) = [(ak + b) \text{ mod }p] \text{ mod }m\)</span> where <span class="nolink">\(a\)</span> and <span class="nolink">\(b\)</span> are random <span class="nolink">\(∈ {0, 1, . . . p − 1}\)</span>,
and <span class="nolink">\(p\)</span> is a large prime <span class="nolink">\((&gt; |U|)\)</span>.</p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">This implies that for worst case keys <span class="nolink">\(k_1 = k_2\)</span>, (and for <span class="nolink">\(a, b\)</span> choice of <span class="nolink">\(h\)</span>):&nbsp;</p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><span class="nolink">\(Pr_{a,b}{\text{ event }X_{k_1k_2} } = Pr_{a,b}{h(k_1) = h(k_2)} =\dfrac{1}{m}\)</span></p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">This lemma not proved here</p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">This implies that:<br></p>
<p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;"><span class="nolink">\( E_{a,b} [\text{ # collisions with } k_1] = E[∑_{k_2}X_{k_1k_2}] \)</span><br></p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;"><span class="nolink">\( = \sum_{k_2} E [X_{k_1 k_2} ] \)</span></p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;"><span class="nolink">\(=\sum_{k_2} \underbrace{\operatorname{Pr}\left\{X_{k_1 k_2}=1\right\}}_{\frac{1}{m}}\)</span><br></p><p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;"><span class="nolink">\(=\dfrac{n}{m}= α\)</span><br><br></p>
<p dir="ltr" style="text-align: left;">This is just as good as above!<br></p></span></div></div><div class="flexsections-activity-page-navigate-back">
        <div class="header backto">
            <a href="https://learn.saylor.org/course/view.php?id=1307#section-36">
                <i class="icon fa fa-arrow-up fa-fw " aria-hidden="true"></i>
                Back to '8.1: Hash Tables\'
            </a>
        </div>
</div></div>

<script>
    document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () {
        const playlistItems = document.querySelectorAll('.playlist-item');
        const currentVideo = document.getElementById('current-video');
        const videoIds = Array.from(playlistItems).map(item => item.getAttribute('data-video'));
        let currentIndex = 0;

        const updateActiveItem = () => {
            playlistItems.forEach(item => item.classList.remove('active'));
            if (playlistItems[currentIndex]) {
                playlistItems[currentIndex].classList.add('active');
            }
        };

        playlistItems.forEach((item, index) => {
            item.addEventListener('click', function () {
                currentIndex = index;
                const videoId = this.getAttribute('data-video');
                if (currentVideo) {
                    currentVideo.src = `https://www.youtube.com/embed/${videoId}?autoplay=1`;
                    updateActiveItem();
                }
            });
        });

        if (currentVideo) {
            currentVideo.addEventListener('ended', function () {
                currentIndex = (currentIndex + 1) % videoIds.length;
                currentVideo.src = `https://www.youtube.com/embed/${videoIds[currentIndex]}?autoplay=1`;
                updateActiveItem();
            });
        }

        updateActiveItem();
    });
</script>

    var uniqid = "69d69c997ef6469d69c9954af16";
    var container = $('#searchinput-navbar-' + uniqid);
    var opensearch = container.find('[data-action="opensearch"]');
    var input = container.find('[data-region="input"]');
    var submit = container.find('[data-action="submit"]');

    submit.on('click', function(e) {
        if (input.val() === '') {
            e.preventDefault();
        }
    });
    container.on('hidden.bs.collapse', function() {
        opensearch.removeClass('d-none');
        input.val('');
    });
    container.on('show.bs.collapse', function() {
        opensearch.addClass('d-none');
    });
    container.on('shown.bs.collapse', function() {
        input.focus();
    });
});

require(['jquery'], function($){
    $(document).ready(function() {
        // Iterate over each delegated-section
        setTimeout(function(){
                $('body:not(.editing) .courseindex .delegated-section').each(function() {
                // Find the courseindex-sectioncontent inside the current section
                const sectionContent = $(this).find('.courseindex-sectioncontent');

                // Check if sectionContent is empty
                if ($.trim(sectionContent.html()).length === 0 || sectionContent.children().length === 0) {
                    // Hide the span with the expand icon class
                    $(this).find('.collapsed-icon').hide();
                    $(this).find('.expanded-icon').hide();
                }

            });
            const $option = $('#id_customfield_edwskilllevel option[value="0"]');
            if ($option.length) {
                $option.text('None'); // Change the text content of the option
            }
            const $edwfocusoption = $('#id_customfield_edwfocusmode option[value="0"]');
            if ($edwfocusoption.length) {
                $edwfocusoption.text('Default'); // Change the text content of the option
            }
        },300);
    });
});

</div></div><div id="mod_book-chapter" class="box py-3 generalbox book_content"><h3>Hashing</h3><div class="no-overflow"><span class="filter_mathjaxloader_equation"><div class="alert alert-primary" role="alert">
Read this section on hashing. It presents a different perspective from previous lectures. As you will see, there is no singular view of hashing or its implementation. As in all things, there are basic concepts but many ways to formulate and apply them.
</div><p dir="ltr">This
    section presents a completely different approach to searching arrays:
    by direct
    access based on key value. The process of finding a record using
    some computation to map its key value to a position in the array is
    called <strong>hashing</strong>. Most hashing schemes place records in the array in whatever order satisfies the needs of the
    address calculation, thus the records are not ordered by value or frequency. The
    function that maps key values to positions is called a <strong>hash function</strong> and will be
    denoted by <strong>h</strong>. The array that holds the records is called the <strong>hash table</strong> and will be
    denoted by <strong>HT</strong>. A position in the hash table is also known as a slot. The number
    of slots in hash table <strong>HT</strong> will be denoted by the variable <em>M</em>, with slots numbered
    from 0 to M − 1. The goal for a hashing system is to arrange things such that, for
    any key value K and some hash function h, <span class="nolink">\(i = h(K)\)</span> is a slot in the table such
    that <span class="nolink">\(0 ≤ h(K) &lt; M\)</span>, and we have the key of the record stored at <span class="nolink">\(HT[i]\)</span> equal to
    K.&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr">Hashing is not good for
    applications where multiple records with the same key
    value are permitted. Hashing is not a good method for answering
    range searches. In
    other words, we cannot easily find all records (if any) whose key
    values fall within
    a certain range. Nor can we easily find the record with the minimum
    or maximum
    key value, or visit the records in key order. Hashing is most
    appropriate for answering the question, "What record, if any, has key
    value K?" For applications where
    access involves only exact-match queries, hashing is usually the
    search method of
    choice because it is extremely efficient when implemented correctly.
    As you will
    see in this section, however, there are many approaches to hashing
    and it is easy
    to devise an inefficient implementation. Hashing is suitable for
    both in-memory
    and disk-based searching and is one of the two most widely used
    methods for organizing large databases stored on disk (the other is the
    B-tree).&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr">As a simple (though unrealistic)
    example of hashing, consider storing n records
    each with a unique key value in the range 0 to <span class="nolink">\(n − 1\)</span>. In this
    simple case, a record with key k can be stored in <span class="nolink">\(HT[k]\)</span>, and the
    hash function is simply <span class="nolink">\(h(k) = k\)</span>. To
    find the record with key value k, simply look in <span class="nolink">\(HT[k]\)</span>.&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr">Typically, there are many more values in the key range than there are slots in
    the hash table. For a more realistic example, suppose that the key can take any
    value in the range 0 to 65,535 (i.e., the key is a two-byte unsigned integer), and that
    we expect to store approximately 1000 records at any given time. It is impractical
    in this situation to use a hash table with 65,536 slots, because most of the slots will
    be left empty. Instead, we must devise a hash function that allows us to store the
    records in a much smaller table. Because the possible key range is larger than the
    size of the table, at least some of the slots must be mapped to from multiple key
    values. Given a hash function <span class="nolink">\(h\)</span> and two keys <span class="nolink">\(k_1\)</span> and <span class="nolink">\(k_2\)</span>, if <span class="nolink">\(h(k_1) = β = h(k_2)\)</span> where β is a slot in the table, then we say that <span class="nolink">\(k_1\)</span> and <span class="nolink">\(k_2\)</span> have a collision at slot β
    under hash function <span class="nolink">\(h\)</span>.&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr">Finding a record with key value <span class="nolink">\(K\)</span> in a database organized by hashing follows
    a two-step procedure:</p>
<ol dir="ltr">
    <li>Compute the table location <span class="nolink">\(h(K)\)</span>.&nbsp;</li>
    <li>Starting with slot <span class="nolink">\(h(K)\)</span>, locate the record containing key K using (if necessary) a collision resolution policy.&nbsp;</li>
</ol>
<p></p>
<hr>
<p>Source: Clifford A. Shaffer, <a href="http://people.cs.vt.edu/~shaffer/Book/C++3elatest.pdf" target="_blank">http://people.cs.vt.edu/~shaffer/Book/C++3elatest.pdf</a><br></p></span></div></div><div class="flexsections-activity-page-navigate-back">
        <div class="header backto">
            <a href="https://learn.saylor.org/course/view.php?id=1307#section-36">
                <i class="icon fa fa-arrow-up fa-fw " aria-hidden="true"></i>
                Back to '8.1: Hash Tables\'
            </a>
        </div>
</div></div>

<script>
    document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () {
        const playlistItems = document.querySelectorAll('.playlist-item');
        const currentVideo = document.getElementById('current-video');
        const videoIds = Array.from(playlistItems).map(item => item.getAttribute('data-video'));
        let currentIndex = 0;

        const updateActiveItem = () => {
            playlistItems.forEach(item => item.classList.remove('active'));
            if (playlistItems[currentIndex]) {
                playlistItems[currentIndex].classList.add('active');
            }
        };

        playlistItems.forEach((item, index) => {
            item.addEventListener('click', function () {
                currentIndex = index;
                const videoId = this.getAttribute('data-video');
                if (currentVideo) {
                    currentVideo.src = `https://www.youtube.com/embed/${videoId}?autoplay=1`;
                    updateActiveItem();
                }
            });
        });

        if (currentVideo) {
            currentVideo.addEventListener('ended', function () {
                currentIndex = (currentIndex + 1) % videoIds.length;
                currentVideo.src = `https://www.youtube.com/embed/${videoIds[currentIndex]}?autoplay=1`;
                updateActiveItem();
            });
        }

        updateActiveItem();
    });
</script>

                // Find the courseindex-sectioncontent inside the current section

            <div role="main"><div id="mod_book-chaptersnavigation"><div class="container-fluid tertiary-navigation">

</div></div><div id="mod_book-chapter" class="box py-3 generalbox book_content"><h3>Hash Functions</h3><div class="no-overflow"><span class="filter_mathjaxloader_equation"><p dir="ltr">Hashing generally takes records
    whose key values come from a large range and
    stores those records in a table with a relatively small number of
    slots. Collisions
    occur when two records hash to the same slot in the table. If we are
    careful - or
    lucky - when selecting a hash function, then the actual number of
    collisions will
    be few. Unfortunately, even under the best of circumstances,
    collisions are nearly
    unavoidable. For example, consider a classroom full of students.
    What is the
    probability that some pair of students shares the same birthday
    (i.e., the same day
    of the year, not necessarily the same year)? If there are 23
    students, then the odds
    are about even that two will share a birthday. This is despite the
    fact that there are
    365 days in which students can have birthdays (ignoring leap years),
    on most of
    which no student in the class has a birthday. With more students,
    the probability
    of a shared birthday increases. The mapping of students to days
    based on their birthday is similar to assigning records to slots in a
    table (of size 365) using the
    birthday as a hash function. Note that this observation tells us
    nothing about <em>which
    </em>students share a birthday, or on <em>which </em>days of the year shared
    birthdays fall.&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr">To be practical, a database organized by hashing must store records in a hash
    table that is not so large that it wastes space. Typically, this means that the hash
    table will be around half full. Because collisions are extremely likely to occur
    under these conditions (by chance, any record inserted into a table that is half full
    will have a collision half of the time), does this mean that we need not worry about
    the ability of a hash function to avoid collisions? Absolutely not. The difference
    between a good hash function and a bad hash function makes a big difference in
    practice. Technically, any function that maps all possible key values to a slot in
    the hash table is a hash function. In the extreme case, even a function that maps
    all records to the same slot is a hash function, but it does nothing to help us find
    records during a search operation.&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr">We would like to pick a hash
    function that stores the actual records in the collection such that each
    slot in the hash table has equal probability of being filled.
    Unfortunately, we normally have no control over the key values of the
    actual records,
    so how well any particular hash function does this depends on the
    distribution of
    the keys within the allowable key range. In some cases, incoming
    data are well
    distributed across their key range. For example, if the input is a
    set of random
    numbers selected uniformly from the key range, any hash function
    that assigns the
    key range so that each slot in the hash table receives an equal
    share of the range
    will likely also distribute the input records uniformly within the
    table. However,
    in many applications the incoming records are highly clustered or
    otherwise poorly
    distributed. When input records are not well distributed throughout
    the key range
    it can be difficult to devise a hash function that does a good job
    of distributing the
    records throughout the table, especially if the input distribution
    is not known in
    advance.&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr">There are many reasons why data values might be poorly distributed.&nbsp;</p>
<ol dir="ltr">
    <li>Natural frequency distributions tend to follow a common pattern where a few
        of the entities occur frequently while most entities occur relatively rarely.
        For example, consider the populations of the 100 largest cities in the United
        States. If you plot these populations on a number line, most of them will be
        clustered toward the low side, with a few outliers on the high side. This is an
        example of a Zipf distribution. Viewed the other way, the
        home town for a given person is far more likely to be a particular large city
        than a particular small town.&nbsp;</li>
    <li>Collected data are likely to be skewed in some way. Field samples might be
        rounded to, say, the nearest 5 (i.e., all numbers end in 5 or 0).&nbsp;</li>
    <li>If the input is a collection of common English words, the beginning letter
        will be poorly distributed.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="ltr">Note that in examples 2 and 3, either highor low-order bits of the key are poorly
    distributed.&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr">When designing hash functions, we are generally faced with one of two situations.&nbsp;</p>
<ol dir="ltr">
    <li>We know nothing about the distribution of the incoming keys. In this case,
        we wish to select a hash function that evenly distributes the key range across
        the hash table, while avoiding obvious opportunities for clustering such as
        hash functions that are sensitive to the highor low-order bits of the key
        value.&nbsp;</li>
    <li>We know something about the distribution of the incoming keys. In this case,
        we should use a distribution-dependent hash function that avoids assigning
        clusters of related key values to the same hash table slot. For example, if
        hashing English words, we should not hash on the value of the first character
        because this is likely to be unevenly distributed.&nbsp;</li>
</ol>
<p dir="ltr">Below are several examples of hash functions that illustrate these points.&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr"><strong>Example 9.5 </strong>Consider the following hash function used to hash integers
    to a table of sixteen slots:&nbsp;</p>
<pre class="prettyprint">int h(int x) {&nbsp;&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; return x % 16;&nbsp;&lt;br&gt;}&nbsp;</pre>
<p dir="ltr">The value returned by this hash function depends solely on the least
    significant four bits of the key. Because these bits are likely to be poorly
    distributed (as an example, a high percentage of the keys might be even
    numbers, which means that the low order bit is zero), the result will also
    be poorly distributed. This example shows that the size of the table M can
    have a big effect on the performance of a hash system because this value is
    typically used as the modulus to ensure that the hash function produces a
    number in the range 0 to M − 1.&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr"><strong>Example 9.6 </strong>A good hash function for numerical values comes from the
    <strong>mid-square </strong>method. The mid-square method squares
    the key value, and
    then takes the middle r bits of the result, giving a value in the
    range 0 to
    <span class="nolink">\(2^r − 1\)</span>. This works well because most or all bits of the key value
    contribute
    to the result. For example, consider records whose keys are 4-digit
    numbers
    in base 10. The goal is to hash these key values to a table of size
    100
    (i.e., a range of 0 to 99). This range is equivalent to two digits
    in base 10.
    That is, <span class="nolink">\(r = 2\)</span>. If the input is the number 4567, squaring yields an
    8-digit
    number, 20857489. The middle two digits of this result are 57. All
    digits (equivalently, all bits when the number is viewed in binary)
    contribute to the
    middle two digits of the squared value. Figure 9.2 illustrates the
    concept.
    Thus, the result is not dominated by the distribution of the bottom
    digit or
    the top digit of the original key value.
</p>
<p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><img src="https://learn.saylor.org/pluginfile.php/10439573/mod_book/chapter/90526/Screenshot%202024-03-11%20at%2016-17-16%20C%203elatest_3.pdf.png" alt="Figure 9.2 An illustration of the mid-square method" width="270" height="146" class="img-fluid atto_image_button_text-bottom"><br></p>
<p dir="ltr"><strong>Figure 9.2 </strong>An illustration of the mid-square method, showing the details of
    long multiplication in the process of squaring the value 4567. The bottom of the
    figure indicates which digits of the answer are most influenced by each digit of
    the operands.</p>
<p dir="ltr"><strong>Example 9.7 </strong>Here is a hash function for strings of characters:</p>
<pre class="prettyprint">int h(char * x) {&lt;br&gt;int i, sum;&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; for (sum = 0, i = 0; x[i] != ’\0’; i++)&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; sum += (int) x[i];&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; return sum % M;&lt;br&gt;}<br></pre>
<p dir="ltr">This function sums the ASCII
    values of the letters in a string. If the hash
    table size M is small, this hash function should do a good job of
    distributing
    strings evenly among the hash table slots, because it gives equal
    weight to
    all characters. This is an example of the <strong>folding </strong>approach to
    designing a
    hash function. Note that the order of the characters in the string
    has no
    effect on the result. A similar method for integers would add the
    digits of
    the key value, assuming that there are enough digits to (1) keep any
    one
    or two digits with bad distribution from skewing the results of the
    process
    and (2) generate a sum much larger than M . As with many other hash
    functions, the final step is to apply the modulus operator to the
    result, using
    table size M to generate a value within the table range. If the sum
    is not
    sufficiently large, then the modulus operator will yield a poor
    distribution.
    For example, because the ASCII value for "A" is 65 and "Z" is 90,
    <strong> sum </strong>will
    always be in the range 650 to 900 for a string of ten upper case
    letters. For
    a hash table of size 100 or less, a reasonable distribution results.
    For a hash
    table of size 1000, the distribution is terrible because only slots
    650 to 900 can possibly be the home slot for some key value, and the
    values are not
    evenly distributed even within those slots.<br>
</p>
<p dir="ltr"><strong>Example 9.8</strong> Here is a much better hash function for strings.</p>
<pre class="prettyprint">// Use folding on a string, summed 4 bytes at a time<br>int sfold(char * key) {&lt;br&gt;unsigned int * lkey = (unsigned int *) key;&lt;br&gt;int intlength = strlen(key) / 4;&lt;br&gt;unsigned int sum = 0;&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; for (int i = 0; i &lt; intlength; i++)&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; sum += lkey[i];&lt;br&gt;// Now deal with the extra chars at the end&lt;br&gt;int extra = strlen(key) - intlength * 4;&lt;br&gt;char temp[4];&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; lkey = (unsigned int *) temp;&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; lkey[0] = 0;&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; for (int i = 0; i &lt; extra; i++)&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; temp[i] = key[intlength * 4 + i];&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; sum += lkey[0];&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; return sum % M;&lt;br&gt;}<br></pre>
<p dir="ltr">This function takes a string as input. It processes the string four bytes
    at a time, and interprets each of the four-byte chunks as a single (unsigned)
    long integer value. The integer values for the four-byte chunks are added
    together. In the end, the resulting sum is converted to the range 0 to M − 1
    using the modulus operator.</p>
<p dir="ltr">For example, if the string "aaaabbbb" is passed to <strong>sfold</strong>, then the first
    four bytes ("aaaa") will be interpreted as the integer value 1,633,771,873
    and the next four bytes ("bbbb") will be interpreted as the integer value
    1,650,614,882. Their sum is 3,284,386,755 (when viewed as an unsigned
    integer). If the table size is 101 then the modulus function will cause this
    key to hash to slot 75 in the table. Note that for any sufficiently long string,
    the sum for the integer quantities will typically cause a 32-bit integer to
    overflow (thus losing some of the high-order bits) because the resulting
    values are so large. But this causes no problems when the goal is to compute
    a hash function.</p>
<p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><img src="https://learn.saylor.org/pluginfile.php/10439573/mod_book/chapter/90526/Screenshot%202024-03-11%20at%2016-18-19%20C%203elatest_3.pdf.png" alt="Figure 9.3 An illustration of open hashing for seven numbers stored in a ten-slot hash table" width="397" height="249" class="img-fluid atto_image_button_text-bottom"><br></p>
<p dir="ltr"><strong>Figure 9.3 </strong>An illustration of open hashing for seven numbers stored in a ten-slot
    hash table using the hash function <span class="nolink">\(h(K) = K mod 10\)</span>. The numbers are inserted
    in the order 9877, 2007, 1000, 9530, 3013, 9879, and 1057. Two of the values
    hash to slot 0, one value hashes to slot 2, three of the values hash to slot 7, and
    one value hashes to slot 9. <br></p>
<p></p></span></div></div><div class="flexsections-activity-page-navigate-back">

        const currentVideo = document.getElementById('current-video');
        const videoIds = Array.from(playlistItems).map(item => item.getAttribute('data-video'));
        let currentIndex = 0;

        const updateActiveItem = () => {
            playlistItems.forEach(item => item.classList.remove('active'));
            if (playlistItems[currentIndex]) {
                playlistItems[currentIndex].classList.add('active');
            }
        };

        playlistItems.forEach((item, index) => {
            item.addEventListener('click', function () {
                currentIndex = index;
                const videoId = this.getAttribute('data-video');
                if (currentVideo) {
                    currentVideo.src = `https://www.youtube.com/embed/${videoId}?autoplay=1`;
                    updateActiveItem();
                }
            });
        });

        if (currentVideo) {
            currentVideo.addEventListener('ended', function () {
                currentIndex = (currentIndex + 1) % videoIds.length;
                currentVideo.src = `https://www.youtube.com/embed/${videoIds[currentIndex]}?autoplay=1`;
                updateActiveItem();
            });
        }

        updateActiveItem();
    });
</script>

    <div id="region-main-box">
        <section id="region-main" aria-label="Content">
            <span class="notifications" id="user-notifications"></span>
                <span id="maincontent"></span>
                <div class="activity-header" data-for="page-activity-header">

            <div role="main"><div id="mod_book-chaptersnavigation"><div class="container-fluid tertiary-navigation">
    <div class="row">
            <div class="navitem">
                <a class="btn btn-link btn-previous" href="https://learn.saylor.org/mod/book/view.php?id=96109&amp;chapterid=90525#mod_book-chapter" title="Previous" aria-label="Previous">
                    <i class="icon fa fa-chevron-left fa-fw " aria-hidden="true" ></i>
                </a>
            </div>
            <div class="navitem ms-auto">
                <a class="btn btn-link btn-next" href="https://learn.saylor.org/mod/book/view.php?id=96109&amp;chapterid=90527#mod_book-chapter" title="Next" aria-label="Next">
                    <i class="icon fa fa-chevron-right fa-fw " aria-hidden="true" ></i>
                </a>
            </div>
    </div>
</div></div><div id="mod_book-chapter" class="box py-3 generalbox book_content"><h3>Hash Functions</h3><div class="no-overflow"><span class="filter_mathjaxloader_equation"><p dir="ltr">Hashing generally takes records
    whose key values come from a large range and
    stores those records in a table with a relatively small number of
    slots. Collisions
    occur when two records hash to the same slot in the table. If we are
    careful - or
    lucky - when selecting a hash function, then the actual number of
    collisions will
    be few. Unfortunately, even under the best of circumstances,
    collisions are nearly
    unavoidable. For example, consider a classroom full of students.
    What is the
    probability that some pair of students shares the same birthday
    (i.e., the same day
    of the year, not necessarily the same year)? If there are 23
    students, then the odds
    are about even that two will share a birthday. This is despite the
    fact that there are
    365 days in which students can have birthdays (ignoring leap years),
    on most of
    which no student in the class has a birthday. With more students,
    the probability
    of a shared birthday increases. The mapping of students to days
    based on their birthday is similar to assigning records to slots in a
    table (of size 365) using the
    birthday as a hash function. Note that this observation tells us
    nothing about <em>which
    </em>students share a birthday, or on <em>which </em>days of the year shared
    birthdays fall.&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr">To be practical, a database organized by hashing must store records in a hash
    table that is not so large that it wastes space. Typically, this means that the hash
    table will be around half full. Because collisions are extremely likely to occur
    under these conditions (by chance, any record inserted into a table that is half full
    will have a collision half of the time), does this mean that we need not worry about
    the ability of a hash function to avoid collisions? Absolutely not. The difference
    between a good hash function and a bad hash function makes a big difference in
    practice. Technically, any function that maps all possible key values to a slot in
    the hash table is a hash function. In the extreme case, even a function that maps
    all records to the same slot is a hash function, but it does nothing to help us find
    records during a search operation.&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr">We would like to pick a hash
    function that stores the actual records in the collection such that each
    slot in the hash table has equal probability of being filled.
    Unfortunately, we normally have no control over the key values of the
    actual records,
    so how well any particular hash function does this depends on the
    distribution of
    the keys within the allowable key range. In some cases, incoming
    data are well
    distributed across their key range. For example, if the input is a
    set of random
    numbers selected uniformly from the key range, any hash function
    that assigns the
    key range so that each slot in the hash table receives an equal
    share of the range
    will likely also distribute the input records uniformly within the
    table. However,
    in many applications the incoming records are highly clustered or
    otherwise poorly
    distributed. When input records are not well distributed throughout
    the key range
    it can be difficult to devise a hash function that does a good job
    of distributing the
    records throughout the table, especially if the input distribution
    is not known in
    advance.&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr">There are many reasons why data values might be poorly distributed.&nbsp;</p>
<ol dir="ltr">
    <li>Natural frequency distributions tend to follow a common pattern where a few
        of the entities occur frequently while most entities occur relatively rarely.
        For example, consider the populations of the 100 largest cities in the United
        States. If you plot these populations on a number line, most of them will be
        clustered toward the low side, with a few outliers on the high side. This is an
        example of a Zipf distribution. Viewed the other way, the
        home town for a given person is far more likely to be a particular large city
        than a particular small town.&nbsp;</li>
    <li>Collected data are likely to be skewed in some way. Field samples might be
        rounded to, say, the nearest 5 (i.e., all numbers end in 5 or 0).&nbsp;</li>
    <li>If the input is a collection of common English words, the beginning letter
        will be poorly distributed.</li>
</ol>
<p dir="ltr">Note that in examples 2 and 3, either highor low-order bits of the key are poorly
    distributed.&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr">When designing hash functions, we are generally faced with one of two situations.&nbsp;</p>
<ol dir="ltr">
    <li>We know nothing about the distribution of the incoming keys. In this case,
        we wish to select a hash function that evenly distributes the key range across
        the hash table, while avoiding obvious opportunities for clustering such as
        hash functions that are sensitive to the highor low-order bits of the key
        value.&nbsp;</li>
    <li>We know something about the distribution of the incoming keys. In this case,
        we should use a distribution-dependent hash function that avoids assigning
        clusters of related key values to the same hash table slot. For example, if
        hashing English words, we should not hash on the value of the first character
        because this is likely to be unevenly distributed.&nbsp;</li>
</ol>
<p dir="ltr">Below are several examples of hash functions that illustrate these points.&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr"><strong>Example 9.5 </strong>Consider the following hash function used to hash integers
    to a table of sixteen slots:&nbsp;</p>
<pre class="prettyprint">int h(int x) {&nbsp;&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; return x % 16;&nbsp;&lt;br&gt;}&nbsp;</pre>
<p dir="ltr">The value returned by this hash function depends solely on the least
    significant four bits of the key. Because these bits are likely to be poorly
    distributed (as an example, a high percentage of the keys might be even
    numbers, which means that the low order bit is zero), the result will also
    be poorly distributed. This example shows that the size of the table M can
    have a big effect on the performance of a hash system because this value is
    typically used as the modulus to ensure that the hash function produces a
    number in the range 0 to M − 1.&nbsp;</p>
<p dir="ltr"><strong>Example 9.6 </strong>A good hash function for numerical values comes from the
    <strong>mid-square </strong>method. The mid-square method squares
    the key value, and
    then takes the middle r bits of the result, giving a value in the
    range 0 to
    <span class="nolink">\(2^r − 1\)</span>. This works well because most or all bits of the key value
    contribute
    to the result. For example, consider records whose keys are 4-digit
    numbers
    in base 10. The goal is to hash these key values to a table of size
    100
    (i.e., a range of 0 to 99). This range is equivalent to two digits
    in base 10.
    That is, <span class="nolink">\(r = 2\)</span>. If the input is the number 4567, squaring yields an
    8-digit
    number, 20857489. The middle two digits of this result are 57. All
    digits (equivalently, all bits when the number is viewed in binary)
    contribute to the
    middle two digits of the squared value. Figure 9.2 illustrates the
    concept.
    Thus, the result is not dominated by the distribution of the bottom
    digit or
    the top digit of the original key value.
</p>
<p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><img src="https://learn.saylor.org/pluginfile.php/10439573/mod_book/chapter/90526/Screenshot%202024-03-11%20at%2016-17-16%20C%203elatest_3.pdf.png" alt="Figure 9.2 An illustration of the mid-square method" width="270" height="146" class="img-fluid atto_image_button_text-bottom"><br></p>
<p dir="ltr"><strong>Figure 9.2 </strong>An illustration of the mid-square method, showing the details of
    long multiplication in the process of squaring the value 4567. The bottom of the
    figure indicates which digits of the answer are most influenced by each digit of
    the operands.</p>
<p dir="ltr"><strong>Example 9.7 </strong>Here is a hash function for strings of characters:</p>
<pre class="prettyprint">int h(char * x) {&lt;br&gt;int i, sum;&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; for (sum = 0, i = 0; x[i] != ’\0’; i++)&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; sum += (int) x[i];&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; return sum % M;&lt;br&gt;}<br></pre>
<p dir="ltr">This function sums the ASCII
    values of the letters in a string. If the hash
    table size M is small, this hash function should do a good job of
    distributing
    strings evenly among the hash table slots, because it gives equal
    weight to
    all characters. This is an example of the <strong>folding </strong>approach to
    designing a
    hash function. Note that the order of the characters in the string
    has no
    effect on the result. A similar method for integers would add the
    digits of
    the key value, assuming that there are enough digits to (1) keep any
    one
    or two digits with bad distribution from skewing the results of the
    process
    and (2) generate a sum much larger than M . As with many other hash
    functions, the final step is to apply the modulus operator to the
    result, using
    table size M to generate a value within the table range. If the sum
    is not
    sufficiently large, then the modulus operator will yield a poor
    distribution.
    For example, because the ASCII value for "A" is 65 and "Z" is 90,
    <strong> sum </strong>will
    always be in the range 650 to 900 for a string of ten upper case
    letters. For
    a hash table of size 100 or less, a reasonable distribution results.
    For a hash
    table of size 1000, the distribution is terrible because only slots
    650 to 900 can possibly be the home slot for some key value, and the
    values are not
    evenly distributed even within those slots.<br>
</p>
<p dir="ltr"><strong>Example 9.8</strong> Here is a much better hash function for strings.</p>
<pre class="prettyprint">// Use folding on a string, summed 4 bytes at a time<br>int sfold(char * key) {&lt;br&gt;unsigned int * lkey = (unsigned int *) key;&lt;br&gt;int intlength = strlen(key) / 4;&lt;br&gt;unsigned int sum = 0;&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; for (int i = 0; i &lt; intlength; i++)&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; sum += lkey[i];&lt;br&gt;// Now deal with the extra chars at the end&lt;br&gt;int extra = strlen(key) - intlength * 4;&lt;br&gt;char temp[4];&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; lkey = (unsigned int *) temp;&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; lkey[0] = 0;&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; for (int i = 0; i &lt; extra; i++)&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; temp[i] = key[intlength * 4 + i];&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; sum += lkey[0];&lt;br&gt;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; return sum % M;&lt;br&gt;}<br></pre>
<p dir="ltr">This function takes a string as input. It processes the string four bytes
    at a time, and interprets each of the four-byte chunks as a single (unsigned)
    long integer value. The integer values for the four-byte chunks are added
    together. In the end, the resulting sum is converted to the range 0 to M − 1
    using the modulus operator.</p>
<p dir="ltr">For example, if the string "aaaabbbb" is passed to <strong>sfold</strong>, then the first
    four bytes ("aaaa") will be interpreted as the integer value 1,633,771,873
    and the next four bytes ("bbbb") will be interpreted as the integer value
    1,650,614,882. Their sum is 3,284,386,755 (when viewed as an unsigned
    integer). If the table size is 101 then the modulus function will cause this
    key to hash to slot 75 in the table. Note that for any sufficiently long string,
    the sum for the integer quantities will typically cause a 32-bit integer to
    overflow (thus losing some of the high-order bits) because the resulting
    values are so large. But this causes no problems when the goal is to compute
    a hash function.</p>
<p dir="ltr" style="text-align: center;"><img src="https://learn.saylor.org/pluginfile.php/10439573/mod_book/chapter/90526/Screenshot%202024-03-11%20at%2016-18-19%20C%203elatest_3.pdf.png" alt="Figure 9.3 An illustration of open hashing for seven numbers stored in a ten-slot hash table" width="397" height="249" class="img-fluid atto_image_button_text-bottom"><br></p>
<p dir="ltr"><strong>Figure 9.3 </strong>An illustration of open hashing for seven numbers stored in a ten-slot
    hash table using the hash function <span class="nolink">\(h(K) = K mod 10\)</span>. The numbers are inserted
    in the order 9877, 2007, 1000, 9530, 3013, 9879, and 1057. Two of the values
    hash to slot 0, one value hashes to slot 2, three of the values hash to slot 7, and
    one value hashes to slot 9. <br></p>

<script>
    document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () {
        const playlistItems = document.querySelectorAll('.playlist-item');
        const currentVideo = document.getElementById('current-video');
        const videoIds = Array.from(playlistItems).map(item => item.getAttribute('data-video'));
        let currentIndex = 0;

        const updateActiveItem = () => {
            playlistItems.forEach(item => item.classList.remove('active'));
            if (playlistItems[currentIndex]) {
                playlistItems[currentIndex].classList.add('active');
            }
        };

        playlistItems.forEach((item, index) => {
            item.addEventListener('click', function () {
                currentIndex = index;
                const videoId = this.getAttribute('data-video');
                if (currentVideo) {
                    currentVideo.src = `https://www.youtube.com/embed/${videoId}?autoplay=1`;
                    updateActiveItem();
                }
            });
        });

        if (currentVideo) {
            currentVideo.addEventListener('ended', function () {
                currentIndex = (currentIndex + 1) % videoIds.length;
                currentVideo.src = `https://www.youtube.com/embed/${videoIds[currentIndex]}?autoplay=1`;
                updateActiveItem();
            });
        }

        updateActiveItem();
    });
</script>

and Open Hashing
While the goal of a hash function is to minimize collisions, some collisions are unavoidable in practice. Thus, hashing implementations must include some form of collision resolution policy. Collision resolution techniques can be broken into two classes: open hashing (also called separate chaining) and closed hashing (also called open addressing). The difference between the two has to do with whether collisions are stored outside the table (open hashing), or whether collisions result in storing one of the records at another slot in the table (closed hashing).

The simplest form of open hashing defines each slot in the hash table to be the head of a linked list. All records that hash to a particular slot are placed on that slot's linked list. Figure 9.3 illustrates a hash table where each slot stores one record and a link pointer to the rest of the list. 

Records within a slot's list can be ordered in several ways: by insertion order, by key value order, or by frequency-of-access order. Ordering the list by key value provides an advantage in the case of an unsuccessful search, because we know to stop searching the list once we encounter a key that is greater than the one being searched for. If records on the list are unordered or ordered by frequency, then an unsuccessful search will need to visit every record on the list. 

Given a table of size M storing N records, the hash function will (ideally) spread the records evenly among the M positions in the table, yielding on average N/M records for each list. Assuming that the table has more slots than there are records to be stored, we can hope that few slots will contain more than one record. In the case where a list is empty or has only one record, a search requires only one access to the list. Thus, the average cost for hashing should be Θ(1). However, if clustering causes many records to hash to only a few of the slots, then the cost to access a record will be much higher because many elements on the linked list must be searched. 

Open hashing is most appropriate when the hash table is kept in main memory, with the lists implemented by a standard in-memory linked list. Storing an open hash table on disk in an efficient way is difficult, because members of a given linked list might be stored on different disk blocks. This would result in multiple disk accesses when searching for a particular key value, which defeats the purpose of using hashing. 

There are similarities between open hashing and Binsort. One way to view open hashing is that each record is simply placed in a bin. While multiple records may hash to the same bin, this initial binning should still greatly reduce the number of records accessed by a search operation. In a similar fashion, a simple Binsort reduces the number of records in each bin to a small number that can be sorted in some other way.

            <div role="main"><div id="mod_book-chaptersnavigation"><div class="container-fluid tertiary-navigation">

            <div class="navitem ms-auto">
